descriptor: The largest living land animal, reshaping Africa's savannas as it feeds, digs for water and walks.

range.summary: Savannas, woodlands, floodplains and semi-deserts across sub-Saharan Africa, with most elephants now in southern and eastern Africa.

regions.name: Okavango and Chobe
regions.note: Northern Botswana and the wider KAZA landscape hold the largest savanna elephant population.

regions.name: Kruger
regions.note: Kruger had only about 10 elephants in 1905; immigrants from Mozambique rebuilt the population.

regions.name: Tsavo
regions.note: Tsavo and its surroundings hold Kenya's largest elephant population.

regions.name: Selous
regions.note: Poaching cut Selous elephants from 38,975 in 2009 to 13,084 in 2013.

regions.name: Zakouma
regions.note: About 4,000 Zakouma elephants were poached between 2002 and 2010, leaving roughly 450.

regions.name: Gourma, Mali
regions.note: Africa's most northerly elephants, a few hundred, migrate across Mali's Gourma semi-desert.

regions.name: The Gambia
regions.note: The Gambia's last recorded elephant was shot in 1913.

regions.name: Assaba, Mauritania
regions.note: Mauritania's Assaba herd, then Africa's most northerly elephants, died out during the 1980s.

regions.name: Majete, Malawi
regions.note: Poachers wiped out Majete's elephants by the early 1990s; 70 were brought back from Liwonde in 2006.

regions.name: Pilanesberg
regions.note: Young elephants from Kruger were released in Pilanesberg in 1981, returning them to the area.

regions.name: Luiana, Angola
regions.note: After Angola's war ended in 2002, elephants recolonised Luiana, rising from 366 in 2004 to 1,827 in 2005.

source.label: African Elephant Status Report 2016 (IUCN SSC African Elephant Specialist Group)

rangeHistory.note: Elephants still range across much of their sub-Saharan range in fragments; Luiana's from date marks recolonisation after near loss in the war.

population.unit: African elephants continent-wide (savanna and forest species combined)

source.label: African Elephant Database (IUCN SSC AfESG), with Douglas-Hamilton 1979 and 1987 and the Ivory Trade Review Group 1989

population.note: Figures before 2006 are expert estimates with large uncertainty, and 1979 may be an overestimate. No continent-wide count separates the two species; the 2016 Great Elephant Census counted 352,271 savanna elephants in 18 countries.

threats.title: Poaching for ivory
threats.detail: Illegal killing surged after 2008 and peaked in 2011, wiping out herds across East and Central Africa.

threats.title: Habitat loss and fragmentation
threats.detail: Farms, fences and settlements cut the migration routes between water and seasonal grazing.

threats.title: Conflict with people
threats.detail: Crop raiding and deaths on both sides lead to retaliatory and control killings.

threats.title: Drought and climate change
threats.detail: Longer dry spells strain water supplies and kill calves in hard-hit populations.

places.name: Chobe National Park
places.note: Huge dry-season herds gather along the Chobe riverfront.

places.name: Amboseli National Park
places.note: Big-tusked elephants in front of Kilimanjaro, studied for over 50 years.

places.name: Kruger National Park
places.note: Large, accessible population with good self-drive roads.

places.name: Etosha National Park
places.note: Pale, dust-coated elephants at floodlit waterholes in a semi-desert.

places.name: Tarangire National Park
places.note: Baobab country where hundreds of elephants crowd the river in the dry months.

sightings.tip: The dry season from June to October concentrates elephants at rivers and waterholes, and thinner vegetation makes them easier to see.

actions.title: Never buy ivory
actions.detail: Antique or new, any ivory sale helps launder poached tusks into legal markets.

actions.title: Support coexistence projects
actions.detail: Beehive fences and early-warning systems keep elephants out of crops without harming them.

actions.title: Travel with responsible operators
actions.detail: Pick lodges and conservancies that share income with communities living alongside elephants.

actions.title: Fund rangers and monitoring
actions.detail: Anti-poaching patrols and aerial surveys are what detect and stop a poaching surge early.
